Seats won in the 1956 election, the basis of the House Historian's 'initial election results', from Wikipedia's infobox and results table (the table is sourced to the Clerk's Election Statistics): 234 D + 201 R = 435, no third-party winner, no vacancy. The 234 Democrats include Minnesota's 5 Democratic-Farmer-Labor members (the district tables list 229 Democratic, 5 DFL and 201 Republican winners). Not the opening-day count: Wikipedia's 85th Congress article begins the Congress at 233 D, 200 R and 2 vacancies. Replaces pol-house-085, whose House Historian row (232 D, 203 R) repeats the 84th Congress's.

The table prints the total as '4363': 436 with footnote 3, so the total is not a checked value. Later changes (deaths, resignations, special elections, party switches) are not included, per the source.

Seats won in the 1960 election, the basis of the House Historian's 'initial election results', from Wikipedia's infobox and results table (sourced to the Clerk's Election Statistics): 262 D + 175 R = 437 (435 plus one seat each for Alaska and Hawaii), no third-party winner, no vacancy. Indiana's 5th was contested: the page's district table lists J. Edward Roush (D) as re-elected at 50.0% to 50.0%, and its winners add up to 263 D (incl. 3 DFL) and 174 R, one seat off the results table's 262/175, which matches that seat counted for Republican George O. Chambers. Wikipedia's 87th Congress article has the seat pass from George O. Chambers (R) to Roush after a House recount in June 1961, and begins the Congress at 263 D, 174 R. Replaces pol-house-087 (the House Historian's 264 D, 173 R, which no other source gives).

The Clerk of the House's political-divisions table ('[ALL FIGURES REFLECT IMMEDIATE RESULT OF ELECTIONS]'), as printed in the Clerk's Statistics of the Congressional Election of November 3, 1998 (p. 53), an edition with a text layer. The same 96th row (House: 435, 277 D, 158 R, no other party, none vacant) is printed in the Clerk's Statistics of the Congressional Election of November 7, 1978 (https://clerk.house.gov/member_info/electionInfo/1978election.pdf, corrected to April 1, 1979; PDF p. 46, in its table of political divisions from 1855 (34th Congress) to 1979-81 (96th Congress)), in its 1984 edition (PDF p. 74) and in its 2000 edition (https://clerk.house.gov/member_info/electionInfo/2000election.pdf, PDF p. 80). The 1978 and 1984 PDFs are image scans with no text layer, so the gate extracts no text from them (their rows were read from the page images, not gate-checked). The row is the result of the November 7, 1978 election, the same basis as the neighbouring rows' 'initial election results'; later changes (deaths, resignations, special elections, party switches) are not included. 277 + 158 = 435 with no other party, so William Carney (NY-1), a Conservative elected as the Republican nominee, is counted among the 158 Republicans, as he is in pol-house-097 (192 R) and pol-house-098 (166 R). Replaces pol-house-096-fix (277 D, 157 R, 1 Conservative), which filed Carney under others, and thereby pol-house-096 (the House Historian's 278 D, 157 R).
Later changes (deaths, resignations, special elections, party switches) are not included, per the source.

The Clerk of the House's political-divisions table ('[ALL FIGURES REFLECT IMMEDIATE RESULT OF ELECTIONS]'), as printed in the Clerk's Statistics of the Congressional Election of November 3, 1998 (p. 53), an edition with a text layer. The same 99th row (House: 435, 253 D, 182 R, no other party, none vacant) is printed in the Clerk's Statistics of the Presidential and Congressional Election of November 6, 1984 (https://clerk.house.gov/member_info/electionInfo/1984election.pdf, corrected to May 1, 1985; PDF p. 74, in its table of political divisions from 1855 (34th Congress) to 1985-87 (99th Congress)) and in the 2000 edition (https://clerk.house.gov/member_info/electionInfo/2000election.pdf, PDF p. 80). The 1984 PDF is an image scan with no text layer, so the gate extracts no text from it (its row was read from the page image, not gate-checked). This row is the election's result, like its neighbours (pol-house-098, pol-house-100), not the opening-day count: its 253 Democrats include Frank McCloskey of Indiana's 8th district, whose election was contested. The Indiana Secretary of State certified Richard D. McIntyre (R) on December 14, 1984; on January 3, 1985 the House resolved that neither McIntyre nor McCloskey would be seated and referred the contest to the Committee on House Administration; on May 1, 1985 it seated McCloskey, 236 to 190, and he was sworn in. The seat was therefore vacant from January 3 to May 1, 1985. These actions are stated in Precedents of the U.S. House of Representatives, vol. 3, ch. 9, sec. 20.1, McCloskey v. McIntyre (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-HPREC-PRECEDENTS-V3/pdf/GPO-HPREC-PRECEDENTS-V3-4-5-7.pdf), and the House Historian's 99th row (pol-house-099) footnotes 'This total includes one vacancy'. 253 + 182 = 435 with no other party, so William Carney (NY-1, Conservative, elected with Republican support) is counted among the 182 Republicans, as in pol-house-097 and pol-house-098. Replaces pol-house-099-fix (253 D, 181 R, 1 Conservative), which filed Carney under others, and thereby pol-house-099 (the House Historian's 253 D, 181 R with one vacancy).

senate.note: Control changed twice in the 107th Congress: Democratic 2001-01-03 to 2001-01-20 (Gore), Republican 2001-01-20 to 2001-06-06 (Cheney), Democratic from 2001-06-06 (Jeffords). The table's summary row lists Republicans first.

The table's first row for the 117th Congress, its opening session (1/3/2021-1/20/2021); the Congress's summary row (48 D, 50 R, 2 I) is the division from January 20, 2021, which is pol-senate-117-from-0120. The vacant seat was Georgia's Class 2 seat until Jon Ossoff (D) was seated after the January 5, 2021 runoff. The 2 Independents (others) caucused with the Democrats. Replaces pol-senate-117, which gave the January 20 division as the start of the Congress.

The table's row from January 20, 2021 (1/20/2021-1/3/2022); the 117th Congress's summary row and its second-session row (from 1/3/2022) give the same 48 D, 50 R, 2 I. The Senate stood 50-50 with the 2 Independents (others) counted with the Democrats, and Vice President Harris's tie-breaking vote gave them the majority. The opening division (January 3-20, 2021) is pol-senate-117-open. Replaces pol-senate-117.
The table lists no change in party balance after January 3, 2026 as of the access date.

The Soviet Union secretly conducted its first nuclear weapon test, RDS-1, on 29 August 1949 at the Semipalatinsk Test Site in the Kazakh SSR.
China's first nuclear test, Project 596, was detonated on 16 October 1964 at the Lop Nur test site in Xinjiang.

nato.claim: NATO was established on 4 April 1949 by the signing of the North Atlantic Treaty, with 12 founding members: Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Iceland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Greece and Turkey joined NATO on 18 February 1952, the first enlargement.
West Germany joined NATO on 9 May 1955, the second enlargement.
Spain joined NATO on 30 May 1982, the third enlargement.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined NATO on 12 March 1999, the fourth enlargement.
Bulgaria, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia joined NATO on 29 March 2004, the fifth enlargement.
Albania and Croatia joined NATO on 1 April 2009, the sixth enlargement.
Montenegro joined NATO on 5 June 2017, the seventh enlargement.
North Macedonia joined NATO on 27 March 2020, the eighth enlargement.
Finland joined NATO on 4 April 2023, the ninth enlargement.
Sweden joined NATO on 7 March 2024, the tenth enlargement.

warsawPact.claim: The Warsaw Pact treaty was signed on 14 May 1955; the pact was disbanded on 25 February 1991 and the treaty disestablished on 1 July 1991.

notes.claim: In September 2026 the US goods and services trade deficit was $105.0 billion, down $0.7 billion from a revised $105.7 billion in August 2026.

In January-September 2026 the US goods and services trade deficit was $92.4 billion, or 12.2 percent, smaller than in the same period of 2025; exports rose $297.3 billion (11.6 percent) and imports $204.9 billion (6.2 percent).

In September 2026 the US recorded goods trade deficits (Census basis) of $28.7 billion with Mexico, $17.9 billion with China, $14.2 billion with the European Union, $7.9 billion with Germany, $4.8 billion with Japan and $4.4 billion with Canada.

The Census Bureau's 2026 table of US trade in goods with China, whose monthly rows run from January to September 2026, gives 2026 totals of $83,516.8 million in US exports to China, $215,008.6 million in imports from China and a balance of -$131,491.8 million (a US deficit).

The Census Bureau's 2026 table of US trade in goods with Mexico, whose monthly rows run from January to September 2026, gives 2026 totals of $297,567.3 million in US exports to Mexico, $481,586.2 million in imports from Mexico and a balance of -$184,019.0 million (a US deficit).

The Census Bureau's 2026 table of US trade in goods with Canada, whose monthly rows run from January to September 2026, gives 2026 totals of $265,874.0 million in US exports to Canada, $304,564.9 million in imports from Canada and a balance of -$38,691.0 million (a US deficit).

The Census Bureau's 2026 table of US trade in goods with Japan, whose monthly rows run from January to September 2026, gives 2026 totals of $74,902.5 million in US exports to Japan, $108,702.9 million in imports from Japan and a balance of -$33,800.4 million (a US deficit).

The Census Bureau's 2026 table of US trade in goods with Germany, whose monthly rows run from January to September 2026, gives 2026 totals of $65,206.2 million in US exports to Germany, $115,164.8 million in imports from Germany and a balance of -$49,958.7 million (a US deficit).

The Census Bureau's 2026 table of US trade in goods with the European Union, whose monthly rows run from January to September 2026, gives 2026 totals of $344,184.2 million in US exports to the European Union, $419,806.3 million in imports from the European Union and a balance of -$75,622.2 million (a US deficit).
China's overall trade surplus grew by 20% from 2024 to a record $1.19 trillion in 2025, even as its surplus with the United States shrank, with exports increasingly going to other countries.
The Wall Street Journal reported on 14 January 2019 that China's 2018 trade surplus with the United States was a record $323.32 billion despite the US tariffs.
According to UNCTAD, around 80% of the volume of international trade in goods is carried by sea, and the share is even higher for most developing countries.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2024 states that over 80% of world trade volume is carried by sea, which is why disruptions at chokepoints such as the Suez and Panama Canals raise costs for the global economy.
UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 states that international maritime transport accounts for over 80 per cent of global merchandise trade by volume.
According to the International Maritime Organization, international shipping transports more than 80 per cent of global trade.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 (Table 1.3) puts international maritime trade in 1970 at 2,605 million tons loaded (all cargoes): 1,440 million tons of tanker trade, 448 million tons of main bulks and 717 million tons of other dry cargo.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 (Table 1.3) puts international maritime trade in 1980 at 3,704 million tons loaded (all cargoes): 1,871 million tons of tanker trade, 608 million tons of main bulks and 1,225 million tons of other dry cargo.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 (Table 1.3) puts international maritime trade in 1990 at 4,008 million tons loaded (all cargoes): 1,755 million tons of tanker trade, 988 million tons of main bulks and 1,265 million tons of other dry cargo.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 (Table 1.3) puts international maritime trade in 2000 at 5,984 million tons loaded (all cargoes): 2,163 million tons of tanker trade, 1,186 million tons of main bulks and 2,635 million tons of other dry cargo.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 (Table 1.3) puts international maritime trade in 2005 at 7,109 million tons loaded (all cargoes): 2,422 million tons of tanker trade, 1,579 million tons of main bulks and 3,108 million tons of other dry cargo.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 (Table 1.3) puts international maritime trade in 2010 at 8,408 million tons loaded (all cargoes): 2,752 million tons of tanker trade, 2,232 million tons of main bulks and 3,423 million tons of other dry cargo.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 (Table 1.3) puts international maritime trade in 2015 at 10,023 million tons loaded (all cargoes): 2,932 million tons of tanker trade, 2,930 million tons of main bulks and 4,161 million tons of other dry cargo.

UNCTAD's Review of Maritime Transport 2019 (Table 1.3) puts international maritime trade in 2018 at 11,005 million tons loaded (all cargoes): 3,194 million tons of tanker trade, 3,210 million tons of main bulks and 4,601 million tons of other dry cargo.
Global maritime trade grew by 2.4% in 2023 to 12.3 billion tons, rebounding from a contraction in 2022.
Maritime trade volumes reached 12,720 million tons in 2024, growing by 2.2 per cent, above the 2013-2023 average growth of 1.8 per cent.

moments.title: Bretton Woods Agreement
moments.claim: Delegates from 44 Allied countries met at Bretton Woods from 1 to 22 July 1944 and signed the Bretton Woods agreement on 22 July 1944; the accords set rules for the international monetary system and established the IMF and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

moments.title: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
moments.claim: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, whose purpose was to promote trade by reducing or eliminating barriers such as tariffs or quotas, was signed by 23 nations in Geneva on 30 October 1947 and applied provisionally from 1 January 1948; it remained in effect until the WTO was established on 1 January 1995.

moments.title: Marshall Plan (Economic Cooperation Act of 1948)
moments.claim: President Truman signed the Economic Cooperation Act, the law behind the Marshall Plan, on 3 April 1948; under the plan the United States transferred US$13.3 billion to 17 European countries in economic recovery programs after World War II.

moments.title: North Atlantic Treaty (NATO)
moments.claim: The North Atlantic Treaty, the legal basis of NATO, was signed in Washington, D.C., on 4 April 1949; the twelve states that signed it became NATO's founding members.

moments.title: Korean War
moments.claim: The Korean War, fought between North Korea and South Korea and their allies, lasted from 25 June 1950 to the ceasefire of 27 July 1953.

moments.title: Treasury-Federal Reserve Accord
moments.claim: On 4 March 1951 the US Treasury and the Federal Reserve announced their accord, an agreement that separated government debt management from monetary policy and laid the foundation for the modern Fed.

moments.title: Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956
moments.claim: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 was signed into law by President Eisenhower on 29 June 1956, authorizing $25 billion to build 41,000 miles of the Interstate Highway System over 10 years, the largest public works project in American history to that time.

moments.title: Treaty of Rome (European Economic Community)
moments.claim: The Treaty of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957 by Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany and in force from 1 January 1958, created the European Economic Community.

moments.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964
moments.claim: The Civil Rights Act of 1964, enacted on 2 July 1964, outlaws discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin, and prohibits racial segregation in schools and public accommodations and employment discrimination.

moments.title: Vietnam War
moments.claim: Following the Gulf of Tonkin incident in 1964, Congress gave President Johnson authority to increase the US military presence in Vietnam without declaring war; direct US military involvement escalated from 1965 and peaked in 1969, when deployment reached 536,000, and US forces were completely withdrawn in 1973.

moments.title: Social Security Amendments of 1965 (Medicare and Medicaid)
moments.claim: The Social Security Amendments of 1965, signed into law by President Lyndon B. Johnson on 30 July 1965, created Medicare and Medicaid.

moments.title: Environmental Protection Agency
moments.claim: The Environmental Protection Agency, the US federal agency for environmental protection, began operation on 2 December 1970 after President Nixon signed an executive order.

moments.title: Nixon shock (end of dollar-gold convertibility)
moments.claim: On 15 August 1971 President Nixon unilaterally cancelled the direct international convertibility of the US dollar to gold, together with wage and price freezes and import surcharges, which effectively rendered the Bretton Woods system inoperative.

moments.title: 1973 OAPEC oil embargo
moments.claim: In October 1973 the Arab oil exporters (OAPEC) announced a total oil embargo against countries that had supported Israel in the Yom Kippur War, first targeting Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States; when it was lifted in March 1974 the oil price had risen by nearly 300%, from US$3 to nearly US$12 a barrel.

moments.title: China's reform and opening up (Open Door Policy)
moments.claim: In December 1978 Deng Xiaoping announced the Open Door Policy, opening China to foreign businesses that wanted to set up there; for the first time since the Kuomintang era, the country was opened to foreign investment.

moments.title: Airline Deregulation Act
moments.claim: The Airline Deregulation Act, signed into law by President Carter on 24 October 1978, deregulated the US airline industry, removing federal control over fares, routes and market entry of new airlines.

moments.title: 1979 oil crisis (Iranian Revolution)
moments.claim: The 1979 oil crisis followed the drop in oil production after the Iranian Revolution: global oil supply fell only about four percent, but the crude oil price more than doubled over the next 12 months, to $39.50 a barrel.

moments.title: Volcker's monetary tightening
moments.claim: On 6 October 1979 Fed Chairman Paul Volcker announced that the FOMC would manage the volume of bank reserves instead of the day-to-day level of the federal funds rate, to rein in inflation; under the restrictive money-supply targets the federal funds rate reached a record high of 20 percent in late 1980.

moments.title: Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (Reagan tax cut)
moments.claim: The Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (the Kemp-Roth or Reagan tax cut), signed into law by President Reagan on 13 August 1981, cut the top marginal income tax rate from 70% to 50% and the lowest from 14% to 11%.

moments.title: Breakup of the Bell System (United States v. AT&T)
moments.claim: After the Justice Department's antitrust lawsuit United States v. AT&T, a settlement finalized on 8 January 1982 ended the Bell System's telephone monopoly; the divestiture of AT&T's local operating companies to the Baby Bells took effect on 1 January 1984 and cut AT&T's book value by about 70%.

moments.title: Plaza Accord
moments.claim: In the Plaza Accord, signed on 22 September 1985 at the Plaza Hotel in New York, France, West Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States agreed to depreciate the US dollar against the franc, the Deutsche Mark, the yen and the pound by intervening in currency markets.

moments.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
moments.claim: On 9 November 1989, after weeks of civil unrest, the East German government announced that all GDR citizens could visit West Germany and West Berlin, and crowds of East Germans crossed and climbed onto the Berlin Wall.

moments.title: Gulf War
moments.claim: The Gulf War was fought by a 42-country coalition led by the United States in response to Iraq's invasion of Kuwait on 2 August 1990; Operation Desert Storm began with the bombing of Iraq on 17 January 1991 and continued until the liberation of Kuwait on 28 February 1991.

moments.title: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
moments.claim: On 26 December 1991 the Soviet Union was formally dissolved and ceased to exist as a sovereign state, after all 15 union republics broke away between 1990 and 1991.

moments.title: Maastricht Treaty (Treaty on European Union)
moments.claim: The Maastricht Treaty, the founding treaty of the European Union, was signed on 7 February 1992 by the twelve members of the European Communities and provided for a shared European citizenship and the eventual introduction of a single currency.

moments.title: North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)
moments.claim: The North American Free Trade Agreement among Canada, Mexico and the United States created a trilateral trade bloc in North America and came into force on 1 January 1994, superseding the 1988 Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement.

moments.title: World Trade Organization
moments.claim: The World Trade Organization, which regulates and facilitates international trade, was established on 1 January 1995 under the 1994 Marrakesh Agreement, succeeding the GATT.

moments.title: Telecommunications Act of 1996
moments.claim: The Telecommunications Act of 1996, signed into law by President Clinton on 8 February 1996, was the first significant overhaul of US telecommunications law in more than sixty years, amending the Communications Act of 1934.

moments.title: Euro
moments.claim: The euro was introduced to world financial markets as an accounting currency on 1 January 1999, replacing the European Currency Unit at a ratio of 1:1; euro coins and banknotes entered circulation on 1 January 2002.

moments.title: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
moments.claim: The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, enacted on 12 November 1999, repealed part of the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933, removing the barriers that kept any one institution from combining investment banking, commercial banking and insurance.

moments.title: September 11 attacks
moments.claim: Early on 11 September 2001 nineteen hijackers took control of four commercial airliners; American Airlines 11 and United Airlines 175 crashed into the North and South Towers of the World Trade Center and American Airlines 77 into the west wall of the Pentagon.

moments.title: War in Afghanistan (2001-2021)
moments.claim: The US-led war in Afghanistan, launched as Operation Enduring Freedom in response to the September 11 attacks, officially started on 7 October 2001 and lasted until 2021.

moments.title: China's accession to the WTO
moments.claim: China became a member of the World Trade Organization on 11 December 2001; after its entry it pursued export-led growth and became a key link in global supply chains.

moments.title: Sarbanes-Oxley Act
moments.claim: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act, enacted on 30 July 2002, is a US federal law that mandates certain practices in financial record keeping and reporting for corporations.

moments.title: Iraq War
moments.claim: The Iraq War began in March 2003 with the invasion of Iraq by a US-led coalition, which overthrew Saddam Hussein's government; US forces were officially withdrawn in 2011.

moments.title: Troubled Asset Relief Program (Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008)
moments.claim: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 became law on 3 October 2008 and created the Troubled Asset Relief Program, which originally authorized $700 billion of spending.

moments.title: Federal Reserve: zero interest rates and asset purchases (2008)
moments.claim: On 16 December 2008 the Federal Open Market Committee set a target range for the federal funds rate of 0 to 1/4 percent, and said the Federal Reserve would purchase large quantities of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities.

moments.title: American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009
moments.claim: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, a stimulus package responding to the Great Recession, was signed into law by President Obama on 17 February 2009; its cost was estimated at $787 billion at passage, later revised to $831 billion.

moments.title: Affordable Care Act
moments.claim: The Affordable Care Act was signed into law by President Obama on 23 March 2010; with its 2010 amendments it was the US healthcare system's most significant regulatory overhaul and expansion of coverage since Medicare and Medicaid in 1965.

moments.title: Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act
moments.claim: The Dodd-Frank Act, enacted on 21 July 2010 as the primary legislative response to the 2007-2008 financial crisis, aims to promote financial stability, end 'too big to fail', prevent taxpayer-funded bailouts and protect consumers from abusive financial practices.

moments.title: Budget Control Act of 2011
moments.claim: The Budget Control Act of 2011, signed into law by President Obama on 2 August 2011, ended the 2011 debt-ceiling crisis and introduced a joint select committee on deficit reduction and automatic budget sequestration.

moments.title: Russian annexation of Crimea
moments.claim: In February and March 2014 Russia invaded and annexed Ukraine's Crimean Peninsula, beginning the Russo-Ukrainian war; the other G8 members suspended Russia from the group and imposed sanctions on Russia.

moments.title: Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
moments.claim: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, signed into law by President Trump on 22 December 2017, replaced the tiered corporate tax rate (from 15% to as high as 39%) with a flat 21%.

moments.title: 2018 US steel and aluminum tariffs (Section 232)
moments.claim: In March 2018 the United States imposed tariffs of 25% on steel and 10% on aluminum from most countries, covering an estimated 4.1% of US imports (the order was signed on 8 March, effective after 15 days); in June 2018 they were extended to the European Union, Canada and Mexico, and trading partners imposed retaliatory tariffs.

moments.title: US-China trade war (2018 tariffs)
moments.claim: On 15 June 2018 the United States declared a 25% tariff on $50 billion of Chinese exports, with $34 billion taking effect on 6 July 2018; China said it would respond in kind with similar tariffs on US imports from the same day.

moments.title: Brexit (UK withdrawal from the EU)
moments.claim: The United Kingdom officially left the European Union on 31 January 2020 after Parliament passed a withdrawal deal, while staying in the EU single market and customs union for an eleven-month transition period.

moments.title: Federal Reserve: emergency rate cut (COVID-19)
moments.claim: On 15 March 2020, citing the coronavirus outbreak, the Federal Open Market Committee lowered the target range for the federal funds rate to 0 to 1/4 percent.

moments.title: CARES Act
moments.claim: The CARES Act, a $2.2 trillion economic stimulus bill responding to the economic fallout of the COVID-19 pandemic, was signed into law by President Trump on 27 March 2020.

moments.title: United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA)
moments.claim: The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) entered into force on 1 July 2020, replacing NAFTA.

moments.title: American Rescue Plan Act of 2021
moments.claim: The American Rescue Plan Act, a US$1.9 trillion economic stimulus bill to speed recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic and recession, was signed into law by President Biden on 11 March 2021.

moments.title: Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act
moments.claim: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, enacted on 15 November 2021, included approximately $1.2 trillion in spending, with $550 billion authorized for new programs or investments on top of $650 billion for existing infrastructure.

moments.title: Russia's invasion of Ukraine
moments.claim: On 24 February 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, starting the largest and deadliest war in Europe since World War II.

moments.title: Federal Reserve: 2022 tightening
moments.claim: On 16 March 2022 the Federal Open Market Committee raised the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/4 to 1/2 percent and said it anticipated that ongoing increases would be appropriate.

moments.title: CHIPS and Science Act
moments.claim: The CHIPS and Science Act, signed into law by President Biden on 9 August 2022, authorizes roughly $280 billion in new funding for domestic semiconductor research and manufacturing, appropriating $52.7 billion, including $39 billion in subsidies for chip manufacturing in the US.

moments.title: Inflation Reduction Act
moments.claim: The Inflation Reduction Act, signed into law by President Biden on 16 August 2022, aimed to reduce the deficit, lower prescription drug prices and invest in domestic energy production; CBO and JCT estimated it authorizes $891 billion in total spending, including $391 billion on energy and climate change.

moments.title: US export controls on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to China
moments.claim: In a rule effective 7 October 2022, the US Bureau of Industry and Security imposed export controls on advanced computing chips and certain semiconductor manufacturing items, to limit China's ability to obtain advanced semiconductor manufacturing capabilities.

moments.title: 2025 'Liberation Day' reciprocal tariffs
moments.claim: On 2 April 2025, which he called 'Liberation Day', President Trump signed Executive Order 14257, declaring a national emergency over the US trade deficit and invoking IEEPA to raise tariffs on nearly all countries to 10% from 5 April, with higher rates for major trading partners from 9 April.

moments.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act
moments.claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law by President Trump on 4 July 2025, contains the tax and spending policies at the core of his second-term agenda and permanently extends the 2017 individual tax rates that were set to expire at the end of 2025.

moments.title: GENIUS Act (stablecoins)
moments.claim: The GENIUS Act, signed into law by President Trump on 18 July 2025, is a US federal law that aims to create a comprehensive regulatory framework for stablecoins.

moments.title: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (IEEPA tariffs struck down)
moments.claim: On 20 February 2026, in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs.

moments.title: 2026 Iran war
moments.claim: Since 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel have been at war with Iran and its regional allies; Iran responded with missile and drone attacks and blocked the Strait of Hormuz.
